tests.title: How do you communicate under everyday pressure?
tests.intro: Answer 10 situations. Choose the response most like you. This tool explores four broad tendencies: clarity, listening, assertiveness and collaborative communication.

dimensions.label: Clear Expression
dimensions.description: You tend to value clear, specific expression. A useful strength is making your message understandable without unnecessary ambiguity.

dimensions.label: Active Listening
dimensions.description: You tend to prioritize listening and understanding before responding. A useful strength is checking meaning rather than relying on assumptions.

dimensions.label: Respectful Assertiveness
dimensions.description: You tend to express needs, limits and disagreement while trying to respect the other person. Assertiveness is not the same as aggression.

dimensions.label: Collaborative Communication
dimensions.description: You tend to connect viewpoints and look for workable shared solutions. This can be especially useful when people have different needs or interpretations.

questions.prompt: When I need something from another person, I usually…
options: State clearly what I need and why.
First make sure I understand their side.
Ask directly while respecting their right to say no.
Look for a solution that works for both of us.

questions.prompt: When someone is explaining something important, I usually…
options: Ask focused questions if something is unclear.
Give them space to finish and listen carefully.
Share my view after I understand the main point.
Summarize what I heard so we can check our understanding.

questions.prompt: When I disagree with someone, I tend to…
options: Explain my position clearly.
Try to understand how they reached theirs.
Express disagreement without attacking the person.
Look for the part of each viewpoint that can move the conversation forward.

questions.prompt: When a conversation becomes tense, I usually…
options: Say what the actual issue is.
Slow down and listen before responding.
State my boundary calmly if needed.
Help shift the discussion toward a workable next step.

questions.prompt: If someone asks me to do something unreasonable, I usually…
options: Explain clearly what I can and cannot do.
Ask questions before deciding how to respond.
Say no respectfully when necessary.
Offer an alternative that is realistic for both sides.

questions.prompt: When I realize I may have misunderstood someone, I…
options: Ask for clarification instead of guessing.
Listen again to their exact meaning.
Admit the misunderstanding directly.
Restate what I think they mean and invite correction.

questions.prompt: When giving feedback, I usually…
options: Describe the specific behavior or issue.
Consider the other person's perspective.
Be honest without using insults or blame.
Discuss a constructive next step.

questions.prompt: When someone criticizes me, I try to…
options: Ask what specifically they mean.
Listen for information before defending myself.
Respond to the point without attacking back.
Separate useful feedback from the emotion of the moment.

questions.prompt: During group conversations, I tend to…
options: Make my point clearly and briefly.
Notice who has not had a chance to speak.
Speak up without trying to dominate.
Help connect different ideas.

questions.prompt: When I am upset, before sending a message I usually…
options: Make sure the main point is clear.
Read it again from the other person's perspective.
Pause if I might say something I will regret.
Think about what outcome I want from the conversation.

guidance.evidence: Moderate-to-strong construct literature; original questionnaire, not psychometrically validated.
guidance.limitations: Self-report responses can be affected by context and social desirability. Communication behavior varies by relationship, power, culture and situation.
recommendations: When a conversation matters, state the specific point you want understood before adding explanations.
Practice reflecting the other person's main point before responding with your own view.
Use a clear request and describe the situation without labeling the other person's character.
reflections: What happens to my communication when I feel rushed or misunderstood?
Which part is harder for me: listening, expressing, or asking clearly?

tests.title: How do you usually respond when disagreement gets difficult?
tests.intro: Explore 10 everyday conflict situations. The questions look at staying engaged, understanding perspectives, expressing your position and moving toward workable next steps.

dimensions.label: Stay Engaged
dimensions.description: You tend to keep the conversation open and attentive. Active listening can help clarify what is actually being disputed.

dimensions.label: Perspective Taking
dimensions.description: You tend to consider the other person's viewpoint and experience. Research on conflict communication links communicated perspective-taking with less defensive responses in some settings.

dimensions.label: Clear Assertiveness
dimensions.description: You tend to express your own position clearly while trying to avoid personal attacks. Research has examined I-language and communicating perspective as ways of reducing perceived hostility in conflict openings.

dimensions.label: Problem Solving
dimensions.description: You tend to move toward concrete next steps and workable agreements. Conflict research also emphasizes that the usefulness of a communication approach depends on the issue and context.

questions.prompt: When a disagreement starts becoming tense, I usually…
options: Stay present and try to keep the discussion focused.
Pause and try to understand what the other person is experiencing.
Clearly explain what I need without attacking the person.
Look for a practical next step we can both work with.

questions.prompt: When I strongly disagree with someone, I tend to…
options: Keep listening even when I disagree.
Ask what might make their position reasonable to them.
State my own view directly and respectfully.
Search for a solution that addresses the main issue.

questions.prompt: If I feel misunderstood during conflict, I usually…
options: Ask questions before assuming what they meant.
Try to understand how my words may have been heard.
Clarify my position using specific examples.
Suggest a concrete way to resolve the misunderstanding.

questions.prompt: When emotions rise, I am most likely to…
options: Stay engaged while slowing the conversation down.
Notice the other person's emotional perspective.
Use clear 'I' language to describe my experience.
Suggest a pause or a next step that prevents escalation.

questions.prompt: When someone blames me, I usually…
options: Listen for the specific problem underneath the blame.
Consider why they may be feeling that way.
Respond to the issue without accepting unfair personal labels.
Bring the conversation back to what can actually be changed.

questions.prompt: When I think the other person is wrong, I try to…
options: Make sure I understand their actual point first.
Consider the information or experience behind their view.
Explain why I see the situation differently.
Identify any part of the problem where we can agree.

questions.prompt: If an argument keeps repeating, I tend to…
options: Stay curious about what has not been understood.
Look for the pattern in both people's reactions.
Name the recurring issue clearly and respectfully.
Work toward a specific agreement or change.

questions.prompt: When I need something from someone after a disagreement, I…
options: Listen to their concerns before making the request.
Consider how the request may affect them.
Say clearly what I need and why.
Suggest a realistic way to make it happen.

questions.prompt: When I realize I contributed to a conflict, I…
options: Stay engaged rather than avoiding the topic.
Try to understand the impact on the other person.
Acknowledge my part directly.
Focus on what I can do differently next time.

questions.prompt: When the other person becomes defensive, I usually…
options: Ask a clarifying question and listen.
Try to understand what they may be protecting or worried about.
Adjust my wording while keeping my point clear.
Look for a calmer, more specific way forward.

guidance.evidence: Moderate-to-strong relationship/conflict literature; original educational questionnaire.
guidance.limitations: Conflict behavior is highly context-dependent. This tool does not assess abuse, coercive control, safety or relationship quality.
recommendations: Separate the problem from the person: describe the specific behavior or decision at issue.
Before defending your position, identify one part of the other person's perspective that you genuinely understand.
If emotions are too high for productive discussion, agree on a specific time to return to the issue rather than disappearing indefinitely.
reflections: Do I tend to pursue, pause, withdraw, or problem-solve first?
What helps me return to a difficult conversation constructively?

tests.title: How Do You Approach Decisions?
tests.intro: Answer 10 everyday scenarios. Notice whether you tend to gather evidence, reflect before acting, choose a practical step, or adapt as new information appears.

dimensions.label: Evidence & Analysis
dimensions.description: You often prefer relevant information, comparison and visible reasoning before choosing.

dimensions.label: Reflection & Confidence
dimensions.description: You often pause to examine assumptions, confidence and possible consequences.

dimensions.label: Practical Action
dimensions.description: You often favor a workable next step, learn from feedback and adjust.

dimensions.label: Adaptive Judgment
dimensions.description: You often update your choice when new evidence or changing conditions make a different response useful.

questions.prompt: When two options both seem reasonable, I usually…
options: Compare the strongest evidence for each.
Pause and ask what I may be overlooking.
Choose a workable option and learn from the result.
Keep the choice open while I look for new information.

questions.prompt: When I do not have enough information, I tend to…
options: Identify what evidence is missing.
Think about how uncertain I feel and why.
Make the smallest useful decision I can.
Wait for information that could meaningfully change the choice.

questions.prompt: Before an important decision, I am most likely to…
options: List key facts and trade-offs.
Check whether my assumptions are sound.
Identify the next practical step.
Consider how the situation could change.

questions.prompt: If new evidence challenges my first choice, I…
options: Recheck the evidence.
Ask why I was initially confident.
Change course if the practical result calls for it.
Update my decision when the new evidence is meaningful.

questions.prompt: When a decision has possible downsides, I usually…
options: Compare likely costs and benefits.
Consider how confident I am about those estimates.
Look for a manageable way to reduce the downside.
Consider which risks change if circumstances shift.

questions.prompt: When pressure makes a decision urgent, I try to…
options: Identify the most important facts first.
Notice whether pressure is narrowing my thinking.
Choose the safest useful next action.
Decide what can be revisited later.

questions.prompt: After making a decision, I am most likely to…
options: Review the evidence that supported it.
Reflect on whether my confidence matched the outcome.
Focus on what happened and what to do next.
Update my approach using the feedback.

questions.prompt: When someone strongly disagrees with my choice, I…
options: Ask which evidence supports their view.
Check whether I may be missing something.
Look for a practical way forward.
Stay open to changing my view if new information matters.

questions.prompt: When the outcome is uncertain, I prefer to…
options: Estimate what is known and unknown.
Think about how much uncertainty I can reasonably accept.
Take a small step that gives useful feedback.
Keep monitoring the situation as it changes.

questions.prompt: If I notice I made an error, I…
options: Identify which information or reasoning failed.
Examine why I was confident.
Correct the practical problem first.
Change my approach for the next decision.

guidance.evidence: Strong theoretical/review literature; original educational questionnaire.
guidance.limitations: Good decisions depend on domain knowledge, stakes, time, available evidence and consequences. A self-report profile does not measure decision accuracy.
recommendations: For high-stakes choices, write down the evidence that could genuinely change your decision before choosing.
Separate confidence from certainty: note what you know, what you infer and what remains unknown.
After an important decision, review the outcome for learning rather than judging yourself solely by whether it worked.
reflections: What evidence would actually make me change my mind?
Do I confuse feeling confident with having strong evidence?

tests.title: How do you work with emotions?
tests.intro: Answer 10 everyday situations. Choose the response that is most like you. This test explores four broad dimensions: noticing emotions, understanding them, regulating responses and using emotional information in relationships.

dimensions.label: Emotional Awareness
dimensions.description: You tend to notice and identify emotional signals in yourself and situations. Greater awareness can create a useful pause between an emotion and a response.

dimensions.label: Emotional Understanding
dimensions.description: You tend to look for triggers, meanings and context behind emotions rather than treating the first interpretation as the whole story.

dimensions.label: Emotional Regulation
dimensions.description: You tend to focus on choosing responses deliberately, especially when emotions are intense. Regulation is not the same as suppressing emotions.

dimensions.label: Interpersonal Emotional Skill
dimensions.description: You tend to consider how emotions operate between people and use that awareness to support clearer, more constructive interactions.

questions.prompt: When I notice a strong emotion in myself, I usually…
options: Recognize and name what I am feeling.
Try to understand what triggered it.
Pause before deciding how to respond.
Notice how it may affect my interaction with others.

questions.prompt: When my mood changes unexpectedly, I tend to…
options: Notice the change fairly quickly.
Look for a possible reason or pattern.
Give myself time before reacting.
Consider whether the change is affecting people around me.

questions.prompt: If someone becomes unusually quiet during a conversation, I usually…
options: Notice the change in their emotional tone.
Consider several possible reasons.
Avoid jumping to a conclusion or reacting impulsively.
Check in respectfully rather than assuming.

questions.prompt: When I feel angry, I am most likely to…
options: Recognize the intensity of the anger.
Think about what the anger is communicating.
Create some space before responding.
Consider how my response could affect the relationship.

questions.prompt: When a difficult emotion keeps returning, I usually…
options: Can identify when it is happening.
Look for recurring triggers or meanings.
Try a healthier way to respond.
Talk about it or seek support when appropriate.

questions.prompt: When receiving criticism, my first useful step is to…
options: Notice my emotional reaction.
Separate the useful message from my assumptions.
Pause so the emotion does not control my response.
Consider the other person's perspective.

questions.prompt: When someone is upset with me, I tend to…
options: Notice the emotional cues in the conversation.
Try to understand what may be underneath them.
Manage my defensiveness before replying.
Listen and respond in a way that keeps the conversation constructive.

questions.prompt: When I am under pressure, I usually…
options: Notice signs that stress is building.
Think about what is driving the pressure.
Use a strategy that helps me regain balance.
Communicate my needs instead of taking stress out on others.

questions.prompt: When two people have different emotional reactions to the same event, I…
options: Notice that their feelings may genuinely differ.
Try to understand each person's interpretation.
Avoid treating my reaction as the only possible one.
Use the difference to improve the conversation.

questions.prompt: Before sending an emotional message, I often…
options: Notice how strongly I am feeling.
Consider what I actually want the message to communicate.
Pause and choose my response deliberately.
Think about how the message may be received.

guidance.evidence: Strong research literature but multiple competing EI models exist; this is an original self-reflection tool, not an EI ability test.
guidance.limitations: Self-report cannot establish ability EI or clinical emotional functioning. Emotional responses are context-dependent.
recommendations: Name the emotion and the situation separately: 'I feel frustrated' is different from 'this person is frustrating.'
Before reacting, identify what the emotion is signaling and what action would fit the situation.
When another person is emotional, first clarify what they need—listening, information, space or practical help.
reflections: Which emotions do I notice quickly, and which do I understand only later?
What usually happens between feeling an emotion and choosing how to respond?

tests.title: What tends to keep you moving toward a goal?
tests.intro: Explore 10 everyday situations. The questions look at personal meaning, choice, persistence, flexibility and the conditions that support your goal pursuit.

dimensions.label: Personal Meaning
dimensions.description: You tend to draw motivation from goals that connect with values or reasons that matter to you personally.

dimensions.label: Choice & Ownership
dimensions.description: You tend to be energized when you have meaningful choice and a sense that the goal is yours to pursue.

dimensions.label: Growth & Competence
dimensions.description: You tend to stay engaged when goals provide opportunities to learn, improve and experience growing capability.

dimensions.label: Support & Structure
dimensions.description: You tend to benefit from supportive people, routines and environments that make consistent action easier.

questions.prompt: When I choose an important goal, I am most energized by…
options: Feeling that the goal matters to me personally.
Having freedom to choose how I pursue it.
Seeing myself improve and become more capable.
Having people or routines that support the effort.

questions.prompt: When a goal becomes difficult, I usually…
options: Reconnect with why it matters to me.
Change my approach while keeping ownership of the goal.
Break the challenge into a skill I can improve.
Seek useful support or adjust my environment.

questions.prompt: I am more likely to keep working when…
options: The goal fits something I genuinely value.
I feel the decision is truly mine.
I can see progress in my ability.
My surroundings make the desired action easier.

questions.prompt: When someone else sets a goal for me, I tend to…
options: Ask how it connects with what I care about.
Want some choice in how I accomplish it.
Focus on learning what would make me capable of it.
Look for support, resources or clear expectations.

questions.prompt: If external rewards disappear, I usually…
options: Continue when the activity still feels meaningful.
Continue when I still feel ownership of the goal.
Continue when I enjoy improving at it.
Look for another structure that helps me stay consistent.

questions.prompt: When progress is slower than expected, I…
options: Remind myself why the outcome matters.
Reconsider the method without abandoning my agency.
Focus on what the experience is teaching me.
Change the routine or support around the goal.

questions.prompt: A goal feels personally meaningful when…
options: It reflects something I value or care about.
It feels chosen rather than imposed.
It helps me grow in competence or understanding.
It connects with people, contribution or a supportive context.

questions.prompt: When I lose momentum, I am most helped by…
options: Reconnecting with the purpose behind the goal.
Making a fresh choice about the next step.
Choosing a small challenge that lets me experience progress.
Changing my environment, routine or accountability.

questions.prompt: If a goal stops fitting my life, I prefer to…
options: Check whether the underlying value still matters.
Give myself permission to choose a different direction.
Ask what I learned that can transfer to another goal.
Discuss the change with people affected by it.

questions.prompt: When I succeed at something difficult, I value…
options: Knowing the achievement mattered to me.
Knowing I chose and directed the effort.
Feeling more capable because of what I learned.
Appreciating the people and conditions that helped.

guidance.evidence: Strong motivation literature; original educational questionnaire.
guidance.limitations: Motivation changes across tasks, environments, resources and relationships. This is not a measure of academic or occupational performance.
recommendations: Connect a difficult goal to a value that matters to you rather than relying only on pressure or rewards.
Break a vague goal into one observable next action and decide when and where it will happen.
Track progress in a way that shows learning and competence, not only final outcomes.
reflections: Which goals feel personally meaningful rather than merely expected?
What kind of support makes action easier without taking away my sense of ownership?

tests.title: Which personality tendencies show up in your everyday life?
tests.intro: Answer 10 everyday situations. Choose the response that is most like you. This original reflection explores five broad personality dimensions often studied in personality psychology.

dimensions.label: Openness to Experience
dimensions.description: You may show greater curiosity and openness toward unfamiliar ideas and experiences.

dimensions.label: Conscientiousness
dimensions.description: You may show greater organization, responsibility and follow-through.

dimensions.label: Agreeableness
dimensions.description: You may place greater emphasis on cooperation, consideration and interpersonal impact.

dimensions.label: Extraversion
dimensions.description: You may be more inclined toward active social engagement and interaction.

dimensions.label: Emotional Stability
dimensions.description: You may show a greater tendency toward emotional steadiness when facing pressure or uncertainty.

questions.prompt: When I meet an unfamiliar idea, I usually…
options: Prefer familiar ideas unless change is necessary.
Consider it briefly if it seems useful.
Become curious and explore what it might mean.
Enjoy exploring it even when it challenges my usual view.

questions.prompt: When a routine gives me a chance to try something new, I…
options: Usually keep the routine unchanged.
Try a small change when there is a clear reason.
Enjoy experimenting with a different approach.
Actively look for new experiences or perspectives.

questions.prompt: When I have an important task, I usually…
options: Start when the deadline becomes close.
Make a rough plan and adjust it.
Set clear steps and monitor progress.
Create a detailed plan and follow through carefully.

questions.prompt: When I make a commitment, I tend to…
options: Need reminders to stay on track.
Usually complete it with some flexibility.
Keep track of what I promised.
Treat follow-through as an important responsibility.

questions.prompt: When someone is treated unfairly, I tend to…
options: Focus mainly on my own position.
Notice the situation but may stay unsure what to do.
Consider the person's perspective before responding.
Make a deliberate effort to respond with fairness and consideration.

questions.prompt: When a disagreement becomes personal, I usually…
options: Focus on defending my own position.
Try to understand the other person's side.
Look for a respectful way to protect both perspectives.
Actively prioritize cooperation and the relationship while discussing the issue.

questions.prompt: In a social setting with unfamiliar people, I usually…
options: Prefer to stay mostly on my own.
Join a conversation if someone invites me.
Often start or join conversations.
Actively seek interaction and enjoy meeting several people.

questions.prompt: After spending time with a group, I often…
options: Prefer quiet time and little further interaction.
Feel comfortable with either more interaction or quiet time.
Usually enjoy continuing social interaction.
Often feel energized by further conversation or activity.

questions.prompt: When several things go wrong at once, I usually…
options: Feel overwhelmed and need substantial time before acting.
Pause and handle one issue at a time.
Usually regain focus after a short pause.
Can often stay composed enough to assess the next step.

questions.prompt: When I receive unexpected criticism, I tend to…
options: React strongly before I have time to process it.
Need some time before deciding how to respond.
Can usually consider the feedback without losing focus.
Usually stay steady enough to examine the feedback and decide what is useful.

guidance.evidence: Very strong construct literature; this short original reflection is not a validated Big Five inventory and has no norms.
guidance.limitations: Personality traits describe tendencies, not fixed identities. Two items per trait cannot provide the precision of established inventories.
recommendations: Interpret trait tendencies as context-sensitive patterns rather than labels or strengths/weaknesses in themselves.
Compare your responses across situations; a trait tendency does not mean you behave the same way everywhere.
Use the result to choose one environment or habit that fits your current preferences rather than trying to change your identity.
reflections: Where does my usual pattern change because the situation changes?
Which tendency helps me in one context but creates friction in another?

tests.title: How do you communicate in close relationships?
tests.intro: Answer 10 everyday situations. Choose the response that is most like you. This reflection explores listening, emotional responsiveness, constructive expression and repair when conversations become difficult.

dimensions.label: Listening & Understanding
dimensions.description: You tend to prioritize accurate listening, clarification and understanding before moving to your own response.

dimensions.label: Emotional Responsiveness
dimensions.description: You tend to pay attention to emotional cues, validation and the experience of the other person during conversations.

dimensions.label: Constructive Expression
dimensions.description: You tend to value direct, respectful expression of needs and concerns without turning disagreement into personal attack.

dimensions.label: Repair & Collaboration
dimensions.description: You tend to focus on repairing misunderstandings, finding workable next steps and keeping difficult conversations productive.

questions.prompt: When someone I care about is telling me something difficult, I usually…
options: Listen without planning my reply while they are speaking.
Try to understand what they are feeling as well as what they are saying.
Share my view clearly after giving them space to speak.
Look for a way to keep the conversation constructive and useful.

questions.prompt: When I realize I misunderstood my partner or loved one, I tend to…
options: Ask what they meant instead of relying on my assumption.
Acknowledge how my misunderstanding may have affected them.
Explain my own perspective without turning it into a defence.
Clarify the issue and work toward a better understanding.

questions.prompt: When someone shares good news with me, I usually…
options: Give them my attention and let them tell the story.
Show genuine interest in why the news matters to them.
Express encouragement in a way that feels natural to me.
Ask questions or respond in a way that helps the positive moment continue.

questions.prompt: During a disagreement, I am most likely to…
options: Listen for the point beneath the words.
Notice when emotions are rising and respond with care.
State my concern directly without attacking the person.
Focus on what could actually change or be agreed upon.

questions.prompt: When I feel hurt by something someone close to me did, I usually…
options: Make sure I understand what happened before reacting.
Try to identify and name what I am feeling.
Explain the impact on me rather than using personal labels.
Discuss what could be done differently next time.

questions.prompt: When the other person becomes defensive, I tend to…
options: Slow down and make sure I have understood their point.
Consider what may be making the conversation feel threatening.
Keep my message specific rather than escalating my language.
Look for a practical way to lower tension and continue later if needed.

questions.prompt: If an important conversation is going nowhere, I usually…
options: Ask questions to find where our understandings differ.
Recognize when both people may need a pause.
Restate my main point more clearly and respectfully.
Suggest a next step instead of repeating the same argument.

questions.prompt: When I disagree with someone I love, I can usually…
options: Accurately summarize their position before explaining mine.
Accept that we may experience the same situation differently.
Disagree without insulting, mocking or dismissing them.
Look for common ground or a workable compromise.

questions.prompt: After I say something that hurts someone, I tend to…
options: Listen to their explanation before deciding what happened.
Take their feelings seriously even if I had a different intention.
Acknowledge my part without shifting all the blame back.
Try to repair the interaction and change the behavior where possible.

questions.prompt: When a difficult topic needs to be discussed, I prefer to…
options: Give both people enough space to speak and clarify.
Choose a moment when emotions can be handled respectfully.
Use direct but non-attacking language.
End with a clear understanding of what happens next.

guidance.evidence: Strong relationship-communication literature; original educational questionnaire.
guidance.limitations: This tool does not assess relationship satisfaction, abuse, coercion, compatibility or safety.
recommendations: Use specific observations and requests when raising a concern instead of global labels such as 'always' or 'never'.
Show responsiveness by acknowledging the other person's experience before moving to your own explanation.
After a misunderstanding, return to the issue and clarify what each person understood rather than trying to win the argument.
reflections: How do I show another person that I understood them?
What makes repair easier or harder after a misunderstanding?

tests.title: Resilience & Adaptability
tests.intro: Explore how you tend to recover, adjust, use support and stay oriented toward what matters when circumstances change.

dimensions.label: Recovery & Regulation
dimensions.description: You tend to make room to recover and regain steadiness after difficult experiences.

dimensions.label: Flexible Adaptation
dimensions.description: You tend to adjust plans, expectations or strategies when circumstances change.

dimensions.label: Purpose & Persistence
dimensions.description: You tend to stay connected to meaningful goals while changing how you move toward them.

dimensions.label: Support & Resource Use
dimensions.description: You tend to recognize when support, relationships or practical resources can strengthen adaptation.

questions.prompt: When a plan I cared about suddenly changes, I usually…
options: Give myself time to settle before deciding what to do next.
Look for another workable route and adjust the plan.
Reconnect with why the goal matters and continue from a new angle.
Ask who or what could help me adapt to the change.

questions.prompt: After a difficult week, I am most likely to…
options: Create space to recover before taking on more.
Change routines that are no longer working.
Keep one meaningful priority in view even if progress is slower.
Reach out to people or resources that can make things easier.

questions.prompt: When something goes wrong unexpectedly, I tend to…
options: Notice my reaction and give myself a chance to regain balance.
Experiment with a different approach.
Focus on the bigger purpose rather than one setback.
Consider whether I need information, advice or practical support.

questions.prompt: If my usual way of solving a problem stops working, I…
options: Pause rather than pushing myself harder immediately.
Try a different strategy or revise the plan.
Ask what outcome still matters most.
Look for someone or something that can add useful resources.

questions.prompt: When facing a long period of uncertainty, I tend to…
options: Protect routines that help me stay regulated.
Adjust expectations as new information appears.
Keep meaningful commitments while allowing the path to change.
Stay connected with supportive people or useful resources.

questions.prompt: After a setback, my most useful first step is often to…
options: Recover enough to think clearly again.
Identify what can be changed next time.
Reconnect with what I am trying to build or protect.
Ask for perspective or practical help when needed.

questions.prompt: When circumstances force me to change direction, I…
options: Give myself permission to feel the disruption before moving forward.
Treat the new situation as a reason to revise my approach.
Keep the underlying purpose while changing the route.
Map the people, tools and information available to me.

questions.prompt: When I make a mistake, I usually…
options: Avoid turning the mistake into a judgment about my whole self.
Use what happened to modify my next attempt.
Remember that one outcome does not define the larger goal.
Talk it through or seek feedback if that would help.

questions.prompt: When stress lasts longer than expected, I tend to…
options: Pay attention to recovery rather than simply enduring it.
Change strategies if the current approach is not helping.
Keep perspective about what still matters to me.
Increase support or use available resources.

questions.prompt: When a challenge feels bigger than my current skills, I…
options: Slow down enough to avoid reacting from exhaustion.
Break the approach into smaller experiments and learn.
Focus on why developing this skill matters.
Seek guidance, collaboration or other resources.

guidance.evidence: Strong and evolving resilience literature; original educational questionnaire.
guidance.limitations: Resilience is not a fixed trait or guarantee of recovery. Context, resources and severity of adversity matter.
recommendations: After a setback, protect enough recovery time to think clearly before demanding more from yourself.
When a strategy stops working, change the strategy while keeping the underlying goal in view.
Identify practical and social resources early rather than treating help-seeking as failure.
reflections: What helps me recover enough to think clearly after a setback?
Which resources do I already have but do not consistently use?

tests.title: How well do you notice your own patterns?
tests.intro: Answer 10 everyday situations. This tool invites reflection on noticing thoughts and feelings, checking assumptions, recognizing patterns and separating observation from interpretation.

dimensions.label: Inner Awareness
dimensions.description: You tend to notice your internal experiences. Awareness of thoughts and feelings can create a useful pause for reflection.

dimensions.label: Metacognitive Reflection
dimensions.description: You tend to examine the beliefs, assumptions and meanings behind your reactions. Metacognition involves awareness of one's own cognitive processes.

dimensions.label: Pattern Recognition
dimensions.description: You tend to look across situations and time for recurring patterns rather than treating each moment as completely separate.

dimensions.label: Reality Checking
dimensions.description: You tend to distinguish observations from interpretations and look for evidence before treating an explanation as fact.

questions.prompt: When I have a strong reaction to something, I usually…
options: Notice what I am feeling before moving on.
Ask myself what thought or assumption may be behind it.
Look for patterns in when this reaction tends to happen.
Separate what I observed from the story I am telling myself.

questions.prompt: When someone gives me feedback, I usually…
options: Notice my first emotional response.
Consider what belief about myself the feedback touches.
Ask whether similar feedback has appeared before.
Check the specific evidence before deciding what it means.

questions.prompt: When I make a mistake, I tend to…
options: Notice how I feel about the mistake.
Examine the thoughts I have about what the mistake says about me.
Look for recurring habits that contributed to it.
Separate the actual mistake from broader judgments about myself.

questions.prompt: When I feel certain that I am right, I sometimes…
options: Notice how strongly I am attached to my view.
Ask what assumptions my conclusion depends on.
Recall whether I have been wrong in similar situations.
Look for information that could challenge my interpretation.

questions.prompt: When my behavior changes around different people, I…
options: Notice the difference in how I feel.
Consider what beliefs or expectations may influence the change.
Look for situations that consistently bring out the pattern.
Distinguish the behavior I can observe from my explanation for it.

questions.prompt: When I feel stuck in a decision, I usually…
options: Notice the emotions that are making the decision difficult.
Ask what fear, value or assumption may be influencing me.
Look for whether the same decision pattern has happened before.
List what I know, what I infer and what I still need to learn.

questions.prompt: When I remember a difficult event, I…
options: Notice the emotion that comes with the memory.
Consider how my current beliefs shape the way I interpret it.
Notice whether my reactions to similar situations repeat.
Distinguish what I clearly remember from what I may be filling in.

questions.prompt: When I receive praise, I usually…
options: Notice how I feel receiving it.
Reflect on whether I believe the positive description.
Consider whether the praise matches patterns I have seen in my behavior.
Check the specific behavior being praised rather than making a global judgment about myself.

questions.prompt: When I am stressed, I try to…
options: Notice early changes in my thoughts, feelings or body.
Ask what meaning I am giving the situation.
Recognize my usual stress patterns.
Separate the situation itself from my interpretation of it.

questions.prompt: When I disagree strongly with someone, I…
options: Notice my emotional intensity.
Ask what personal value or assumption may be involved.
Consider whether this type of disagreement repeats for me.
Try to identify what the other person actually said before interpreting it.

guidance.evidence: Strong conceptual and metacognitive literature; original educational questionnaire.
guidance.limitations: Self-report awareness is not the same as objective accuracy. People can be confident about a self-judgment and still be mistaken.
recommendations: When making a self-judgment, separate observation from interpretation: record what happened before deciding what it means.
Check important beliefs against evidence or feedback rather than relying only on how convincing they feel.
Notice repeated triggers and responses across several situations before drawing a conclusion about yourself.
reflections: Which self-beliefs have I actually checked against evidence?
What patterns do I notice only after someone gives me feedback?

tests.title: Stress Response Style
tests.intro: Explore how you tend to notice stress, interpret pressure, regulate reactions and choose coping responses.

dimensions.label: Stress Awareness
dimensions.description: You tend to notice changes in body, mood or attention when pressure rises.

dimensions.label: Situation Appraisal
dimensions.description: You tend to examine meaning, controllability and available resources.

dimensions.label: Regulation & Recovery
dimensions.description: You tend to create space to settle reactions and recover.

dimensions.label: Adaptive Coping
dimensions.description: You tend to adjust coping according to the problem, emotions, support and context.

questions.prompt: When pressure starts building, I usually…
options: Notice changes in my body, mood or concentration.
Ask what the situation means and how serious it really is.
Pause and use something that helps me settle.
Consider what response fits the situation best.

questions.prompt: When I feel overwhelmed, I tend to…
options: Separate what I can control from what I cannot.
Notice signs that I am becoming overloaded.
Choose between action, support or a break.
Give myself time to calm down before the next move.

questions.prompt: If my thoughts speed up, I usually…
options: Recognize that my stress level has changed.
Use a calming practice or create some space.
Ask what is driving the reaction and whether my interpretation is accurate.
Decide what response is useful right now.

questions.prompt: When a stressful problem cannot be solved immediately, I…
options: Look for a workable next step.
Reassess what the problem actually requires.
Use recovery time so pressure does not take over everything.
Notice how the unresolved problem affects my mood and attention.

questions.prompt: When I receive stressful news, I first…
options: Check the facts and what the news means for me.
Notice my immediate emotional and physical reaction.
Give myself a moment before responding.
Think about whether I need action, information, support or time.

questions.prompt: When I cannot control an important outcome, I…
options: Shift attention to what I can influence.
Remind myself that interpretation affects experience.
Notice when uncertainty is increasing my stress.
Use a coping or recovery activity to stay grounded.

questions.prompt: During a busy period, I am most likely to…
options: Notice early signs that stress is accumulating.
Adjust priorities or ask for practical help.
Protect some time for recovery.
Reconsider whether every demand needs the same urgency.

questions.prompt: After a stressful event, I tend to…
options: Take time to settle physically and emotionally.
Reflect on signs of stress I noticed.
Think about what I can learn or change next time.
Review what the event meant and whether my assumptions were accurate.

questions.prompt: When someone gives me stressful feedback, I…
options: Consider what the feedback means before responding.
Regulate my reaction so I can listen.
Look for a useful action or clarification.
Notice what emotions or body signals it triggered.

questions.prompt: If the same stressor keeps returning, I…
options: Look for a practical change to reduce it.
Examine my interpretation, expectations or boundaries.
Track early warning signs so I can respond sooner.
Strengthen recovery and support rather than simply pushing through.

guidance.evidence: Strong stress-and-coping literature; original educational questionnaire.
guidance.limitations: This does not screen for anxiety, depression, PTSD or any other disorder. Stress responses vary with severity, duration, health, environment and available support.
recommendations: When pressure rises, identify what is controllable, what is not, and what the next useful action is.
Use recovery as part of coping: sleep, pauses, movement, social connection or other healthy routines can create space for regulation.
Match coping to the problem: change what can be changed and use emotional support when the situation cannot be immediately solved.
reflections: What signs tell me that pressure is beginning to affect my thinking or behavior?
Which coping responses help me address the situation rather than only distract from it?
